title: Chapter 3: Version Control, Git Internals, and Team Collaboration

blocks.text: Version control is the bedrock of professional engineering. In collaborative software teams and university tech clubs, code that is not tracked in Git does not exist. Git is not simply a cloud backup utility; it is a distributed, content-addressable cryptographic filesystem designed to manage the evolution of source code.
The Git Mental Model: Snapshots, Not Deltas

Many beginners mistakenly believe Git records line-by-line differences (diffs) across files over time. In reality, Git conceptualizes its data as a series of complete **snapshots** of a mini filesystem. Every time you commit, Git takes a picture of what all your files look like at that moment and stores a reference to that snapshot. If a file has not changed, Git does not store it again; it simply links to the previously stored identical blob.

blocks.text: The Three Core Git Objects
Inside the hidden `.git/objects` directory, Git stores three primary data types addressed by their 40-character SHA-1 (or 64-character SHA-256) hash:

blocks.title: Key Highlights
lines: • **Blob**: Raw file content (bytes). A blob contains no filename, directory information, or timestamp—only the content.
• **Tree**: Represents a directory. It points to blobs (files) and other trees (subdirectories), along with their permissions and filenames.
• **Commit**: An object containing a pointer to the top-level root tree, metadata (author, committer, timestamp, message), and parent commit hash(es).

blocks.text: Essential Command Line Workflow
Initialization and Everyday Cycle

blocks.code:
# Initialize a new Git repository in the current folder
git init

# Check the working tree status (untracked, staged, modified)
git status

# Stage specific files or all modified files in the working directory
git add main.py
git add .               # Stages all changes from current directory downward

# Review what changes are staged versus unstaged
git diff                # Unstaged modifications
git diff --staged       # Staged changes ready to be committed

# Record snapshot with an informative commit message
git commit -m "feat(data): implement initial polars CSV ingestion pipeline"

# View concise, graphical commit history
git log --oneline --graph --decorate --all
blocks.caption: Initializing and Tracking Projects

blocks.text:
**The Conventional Commits Standard:**
High-performing engineering teams enforce structured commit messages following the Conventional Commits specification:
`<type>(<optional scope>): <short description>`
\begin{itemize}
 \item `feat`: A new feature or capability.
 \item `fix`: A bug fix.
 \item `docs`: Documentation changes only.
 \item `refactor`: Code change that neither fixes a bug nor adds a feature.
 \item `perf`: A code change that improves performance.
 \item `test`: Adding missing tests or correcting existing tests.
\end{itemize}
Branching, Merging, and Conflict Resolution
In Git, a **branch** is merely an 8-byte pointer containing the commit hash of its tip. Creating or deleting a branch takes less than one millisecond, regardless of repository size.

blocks.code:
# Create and switch to a new feature branch
git switch -c feature/hand-tracking
# (Equivalently: git checkout -b feature/hand-tracking)

# List all local branches (* denotes currently checked out)
git branch

# Switch back to the primary branch
git switch main

# Merge the completed feature branch into main
git merge feature/hand-tracking

# Delete feature branch after successful integration
git branch -d feature/hand-tracking
blocks.caption: Branch Creation, Switching, and Merging

blocks.text: Resolving Merge Conflicts
When two branches modify the same lines of a file, Git halts the merge and injects conflict markers into the offending files:

blocks.code:
<<<<<<< HEAD (Current Branch: main)
std::cout << "Starting server on port 8080..." << std::endl;
=======
std::cout << "Starting high-performance server on port 9000..." << std::endl;
>>>>>>> feature/port-configuration
blocks.caption: Git Merge Conflict Markers

blocks.text: To resolve the conflict:

blocks.title: Key Highlights
lines: • Open the file in an editor (VS Code, Vim).
• Decide which logic to preserve or synthesize both.
• Stage the resolved file: `git add server.cpp`.
• Finalize the merge: `git commit -m "merge: resolve port collision between main and feature"`.

blocks.text: Connecting to Remote Repositories and GitHub Profile
To link your local machine to GitHub securely, configure an SSH key:

blocks.code:
# Generate modern Ed25519 SSH key pair
ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "ulhas@example.com"

# Display public key to paste into GitHub Settings -> SSH Keys
cat ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub

# Add remote origin and push branch
git remote add origin git@github.com:Ulhas123/ai-perception-engine.git
git branch -M main
git push -u origin main
blocks.caption: Generating SSH Keys and Pushing to Remote

blocks.text: Architecting a Professional GitHub Profile (\texttt{github.com/Ulhas123

)}
Your GitHub profile is your engineering resume. A 1st-year student whose profile contains clean documentation and well-structured repositories immediately stands out.

blocks.title: Key Highlights
lines: • **Special Profile Repository**: Create a public repository named exactly `Ulhas123` containing a top-level `README.md`. GitHub renders this file on your user home page.

• **Repository Anatomy**: Every public project must include:
 \begin{enumerate}
• `.gitignore`: Exclude virtualenvs (`.venv/`), build artifacts (`*.o`, `build/`), and environment secrets (`.env`).
• `README.md`: Must have a clear title, badges, architecture diagram or system overview, installation prerequisites, and a quick-start code snippet.

blocks.text: \end{itemize}

**Question**: *“What is the difference between `git merge` and `git rebase`? When should we use which in our club repo?”*
**Defense**: *“`git merge` creates a new 3-way merge commit that preserves the complete historical topology of when branches diverged and re-joined. `git rebase` rewrites commit history by transplanting local commits one by one on top of the latest upstream commit, creating a clean linear history. In shared public branches (`main`), we avoid rebasing because rewriting public commit hashes breaks other teammates' local trees. For private local feature branches, rebasing keeps history pristine before submitting a Pull Request.”*

**Pitfall: Committing API Keys or 2GB Datasets into Git:**
Git retains every object committed in `.git/objects` indefinitely, even if you run `git rm secret.env` in the next commit. If pushed to GitHub, automated scanners scrape exposed keys within seconds.
**Remedy**: Never commit before creating a robust `.gitignore`. If secrets or huge datasets were committed locally, use `git reset –soft HEAD~ 1` to uncommit without losing local code, add the file to `.gitignore`, and recommit.
